implementation_notes: The async default: tokio::spawn creates one task that owns the servant and loops over an mpsc::Receiver<Command>, where every command carries the method arguments plus a oneshot::Sender<T> reply - the closest analogue of the pattern's Future, awaited by the caller. The bounded mpsc channel provides back-pressure, the runtime schedules the task, and the servant needs no locks because it is owned by exactly one task. Blocking work must be pushed to spawn_blocking so it does not starve the runtime.
pitfalls: Blocking calls inside the task (std::thread::sleep, synchronous file I/O) starve the runtime; use tokio::task::spawn_blocking.
If the caller drops the oneshot receiver the servant's send fails: treat that as normal cancellation, not as a panic condition.
The task ends when every sender drops; without a shutdown command queued work is abandoned mid-flight.

variants.name: std thread + mpsc channels (no async runtime)
variants.implementation_notes: Without an async runtime the roles are built from std alone: thread::spawn runs the scheduler loop, std::sync::mpsc (sync_channel for a bounded queue) carries commands, and a per-request reply channel stands in for the Future, with the caller blocking in recv(). The servant is owned by the worker thread and needs no locks. Choose it for CLI tools and services without tokio, especially when the servant performs blocking work that would otherwise need spawn_blocking.
pitfalls: A sync_channel blocks the sender when full: that is back-pressure, but it deadlocks if the caller holds a resource the servant needs to drain the queue.
std mpsc is multi-producer/single-consumer: replies need one channel per request, never a shared reply channel.
The worker exits only when all senders drop; keep ownership of the last sender (or send a shutdown command) so the thread does not leak.
